issues.legal_issue: A conviction for sexual offences may rest on the sole testimony of the complainant only when that testimony is reliable and trustworthy; materially contradictory and unsupported testimony that does not meet that standard cannot sustain conviction.
material_facts: The conviction rested solely on the complainant’s testimony; the other witnesses did not support the prosecution.
The complainant’s account contained material contradictions, including about how the incident occurred and whether she first made an oral or written complaint.
The account of identifying the accused by mobile-phone light was unsupported by recovery of a phone, and the alleged broken boundary wall was not established.
The medical evidence disclosed no physical or pathological evidence of rape, and the forensic findings concerning blood and semen were inconclusive.
There was an admitted land dispute and enmity between the accused and the complainant’s family.
The complainant’s version was not supported by other evidence, and the courts below had convicted the accused on that version.
issues.conclusion: The complainant’s sole testimony was not sufficiently reliable to sustain the conviction. The appeal was allowed, the convictions and sentences were set aside, and the accused was acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: A complainant’s testimony in a rape case can by itself support a conviction, and corroboration is not invariably required, but the testimony must inspire confidence and be reliable, trustworthy, unblemished and of sterling quality. It is not to be accepted as gospel truth without scrutiny. Raju v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2008) 15 SCC 133 explains that the testimony is assessed as that of an injured witness, without an irrebuttable presumption of truth; Rai Sandeep alias Deepu v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2012) 8 SCC 21 describes the standard for a sterling witness; and Krishna Kumar Malik v. State of Haryana (2011) 7 SCC 130 confirms that solitary testimony suffices only when it inspires confidence and is absolutely trustworthy. The Court also referred to Sections 375 and 376 of the Penal Code and Section 114-A of the Evidence Act, noting the restricted scope of the latter’s presumption.

rule.if: appeal_against_conviction and conviction_based_on_solitary_complainant_testimony and material_contradictions and account_not_credible and (medical_evidence_unsupportive or forensic_evidence_inconclusive) and other_evidence_not_supportive

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed from a conviction for sexual offences.
predicates.conviction_based_on_solitary_complainant: The courts based the conviction on the complainant’s testimony alone.
predicates.material_contradictions: The complainant gave materially inconsistent accounts of the incident or its reporting.
predicates.account_not_credible: The court found the described manner of occurrence not believable and the testimony insufficiently reliable.
predicates.medical_evidence_unsupportive: The medical examination did not support the allegation of rape.
predicates.forensic_evidence_inconclusive: The forensic findings concerning the relevant biological material did not establish the allegation.
predicates.other_evidence_not_supportive: Other witnesses or evidence did not support the complainant’s account.

issues.definition: When an appeal from conviction rests on the complainant’s materially contradictory and not credible sole testimony, and the medical or forensic evidence and other evidence do not support it, the conviction cannot stand and the accused is entitled to acquittal.
